The core concept of levered means-end relations formalizes how an organism interacts with one object to influence another, structurally analogous to mechanical leverage. This relation is defined by a distance correlation function d(x₁, x₂), where x₁ and x₂ represent positions of successive means-objects. The mathematical structure implies a dualistic symmetry: motion at one end correlates with motion at the other. In GSI, this translates into Bayesian inference over causal chains, where each step in the hierarchy is treated as a conditional update. In GSE, it becomes a state transition model where each levered interaction modifies the agent’s internal representation of affordances. The failure mode arises when d(x₁, x₂) vanishes or becomes non-invertible, indicating breakdown in tool efficacy or cognitive misalignment. Tool use extends this framework into higher-order hierarchies, where the same lever principle applies recursively across multiple steps. These hierarchies are modeled as Markovian processes in GSI and as path-dependent state machines in GSE. Adaptive behavior emerges when these systems learn to optimize d(x₁, x₂) through repeated exposure, forming a kernel of behavioral optimization.
